claim: The accuracy/robustness dilemma is the structural tradeoff that dynamics-based impedance control can reproduce a desired endpoint impedance accurately only when the robot model is accurate, whereas position-based impedance control attenuates model error through a high-gain inner position loop but allows the resulting inner-loop dynamics to contaminate the desired impedance and can even lose contact. The proposed method restructures the controller as an internal-model-control loop whose internal model is the desired impedance itself, then uses time-delay estimation to compensate unknown nonlinear robot dynamics from one-step-delayed input and acceleration. In the zero-feedback-delay idealization the IMC correction cancels dynamics-estimation error without inserting a competing impedance; with sampled delay, the residual impedance error is filtered by a factor proportional to 1-exp(-Ls), so accuracy is improved but not perfect. A conditional L-infinity stability theorem and 2-DOF SCARA experiments support bounded, more accurate and payload-robust behavior, but the method remains constrained by time-delay-estimation smoothness, sampling and sensor resolution, gain-region tradeoffs, acceleration estimation, and the tested single-contact setting.
claim_locator: Abstract and Section I; Section II-A-E, Eqs. 1-28 and Fig. 1; Section III-A-E, Eqs. 29-66 and Figs. 2-4; Section IV-A-D, Eqs. 67-73, Tables I-II and Figs. 5-12; Section V, Eqs. 74-77 and Fig. 13; Section VI; Appendix Stability Theorem, Eqs. 78-93.
epistemic_status: Full-text primary controller-design and experimental-comparison study. Algebraic accuracy relations and the L-infinity stability condition are theorem- or derivation-supported under stated assumptions; experimental superiority is author-reported for the described SCARA task and was not independently reproduced.
problem_and_setting: Desired impedance is a Cartesian mass-damper-spring relation between trajectory error and interaction force. Direct dynamics-based implementation depends on estimated inertia, Coriolis, centrifugal, gravity, and friction terms and has no independent gain for suppressing model error; sensitivity is especially high for small desired stiffness and large desired mass. Position-based implementation improves robustness by commanding an inner position servo, but model error excites the inner-loop dynamics, which generally differ from the target impedance, degrading force-motion accuracy and potentially causing oscillation or contact loss. The paper seeks simultaneous accuracy, robustness to modeling error, and a simple implementation that avoids full online robot-model computation.
method_or_mechanism: The proposed architecture recognizes dynamics-based impedance control as an internal-model-control-compatible plant. A parallel IMC path uses the desired impedance inverse as controller and the desired impedance as internal model, so the difference between actual and model response feeds back an estimate-error correction. The IMC loop requires only desired mass, damping, and stiffness. Full robot dynamics compensation is replaced by time-delay estimation: Cartesian dynamics are partitioned into a chosen known inertia matrix Mbar_x times acceleration plus an unknown term H containing inertia mismatch, nonlinear dynamics, and interaction force. Assuming H is continuous or piecewise continuous and the delay L is sufficiently small, H(t) is approximated by the previous-step value Fu(t-L)-Mbar_x*x_ddot(t-L). The resulting torque command uses the Jacobian transpose, current desired impedance command, and one-step-delayed force and acceleration information. A recursive reformulation removes explicit real-time integration of the internal-model state. A diagonal forgetting-factor matrix attenuates accumulated quantization error in the recursive IMC feedback, while a first-order low-pass filter may be used in the TDE loop. The ideal no-delay algebra gives exact target impedance independent of dynamics-estimation error; the implementable delayed form leaves an error proportional to the delayed difference of TDE error.
content_summary: The paper first formalizes the dilemma using a nonlinear multi-axis robot. In dynamics-based impedance control, model error enters through the desired impedance dynamics directly, so exact target behavior is fragile. In position-based impedance control, adjustable inner-loop PD gains attenuate model error, but the inverse inner-loop dynamics remain in the error channel and corrupt the commanded impedance. Instantaneous-model impedance control retains this contamination. The proposed IMC structure adds a parallel model identical to the desired impedance, producing a correction term based only on dynamics-estimation error. With no feedback delay, the derived reference-position error is zero even when model error is present. With discrete delay L, the response error becomes the target-impedance inverse multiplied by (1-exp(-Ls)) and TDE error, which attenuates slowly varying error without adding a foreign inner-loop impedance. TDE avoids full dynamics parameters but needs Mbar_x, the Jacobian, recent input force, and numerically estimated acceleration. The practical recursive implementation eliminates the internal model state, adds forgetting factors to suppress cumulative quantization error, and may filter the TDE signal. The L-infinity theorem assumes bounded desired trajectory derivatives and external force and requires the induced-norm mismatch between Mbar_x and actual Cartesian inertia to be smaller than a bound determined by the forgetting-factor matrix. Larger forgetting factors strengthen IMC correction but shrink the admissible Mbar_x stability region, exposing a remaining stability-versus-robustness tradeoff. Experiments use a 2-DOF SCARA-type robot at 1 kHz against an aluminum plate of about 150000 N/m. The task approaches the wall along y, moves 0.15 m along x while maintaining contact, and then holds. The desired impedance is 20 kg, 900 N s/m, and 400 N/m per axis, with damping ratio 5. Without payload, the proposed controller has the smallest free-space deviation, impact force of 57.6 N versus 70.2 N for position-based control, smallest contact-force fluctuation, and smallest impedance error; position-based control reportedly loses wall contact six times. Dynamics-based and instantaneous-model controllers have excessive free-space deviation and are excluded from further task comparison. With a 3.11 kg endpoint payload, the proposed controller again has the smallest position deviation, force fluctuation, and impedance error. Against a disturbance-observer implementation, the additional IMC loop improves results; below the 3.7 Hz motor torque-ripple peak, force PSD is reported at about 30% of the DOB controller's, while high-frequency fluctuation is limited by hardware torque ripple.
synthesis_role: Robust-realization card in the development of impedance control. It separates the desired impedance from the error-correction dynamics, combines target-model IMC with model-light TDE, and shows that robustness need not be purchased by inserting an arbitrary high-gain inner position impedance. It also documents that sampled implementation replaces ideal cancellation with bounded residual error and a gain-dependent stability region.
development_link: Classic impedance control established a continuous force-motion target and later contact-stability work tuned damping against environment stiffness and delay. This work addresses a different bottleneck: reproducing the chosen impedance accurately when robot dynamics are uncertain. It progresses from full model cancellation or inner-position-loop robustness to a two-degree-of-freedom architecture that independently specifies command response and error correction, using recent data instead of full dynamics. It does not choose the impedance, adapt it to task context, or prove general contact-transition safety; later adaptive and learning methods still need to manage parameter selection, nonlinear and multi-contact environments, sampling-energy effects, and estimator uncertainty.

evidence.statement: DB-IC attains the desired impedance accurately with precise dynamics compensation but directly transmits modeling error through the desired-impedance dynamics and lacks an independent correction gain.
evidence.support_scope: Section II-C and II-E, Eqs. 6-21 and Fig. 1(a).

evidence.statement: PB-IC attenuates model error with adjustable inner-loop gains, but model error excites inner-loop dynamics C^-1(s), which contaminate the desired impedance and can cause contact loss or oscillation.
evidence.support_scope: Section II-D and II-E, Eqs. 22-25 and Fig. 1(b).

evidence.statement: The proposed IMC uses the desired impedance as internal model and its inverse as IMC controller, adding a parallel correction term that depends only on dynamics-estimation error.
evidence.support_scope: Section III-A and III-C, Eqs. 29 and 33-40; Figs. 2-3.

evidence.statement: In the ideal no-delay IMC relation, desired impedance is realized exactly regardless of dynamics-estimation error, conditional on closed-loop stability.
evidence.support_scope: Section III-A and III-C, Eqs. 29 and 37-40.

evidence.statement: TDE estimates the unknown nonlinear dynamics from one-step-delayed Cartesian input force and acceleration, assuming the unknown term is continuous or piecewise continuous and L is sufficiently small.
With implementation delay, the impedance response error is proportional to the target dynamics inverse times (1-exp(-Ls)) and TDE error, so cancellation is effective but not exact for finite L.

The recursive controller removes real-time internal-model-state computation, but sensor quantization accumulates through IMC feedback; forgetting factors and low-pass filtering are introduced to attenuate it.
The stability theorem gives L-infinity stability for bounded desired trajectory, derivatives, and external force when the induced-norm inertia-mismatch condition in Eq. 80 is satisfied.
The admissible Mbar_x region depends on the forgetting factor; stronger IMC feedback can improve robustness but reduce the certified stability region.
Experiments use a 2-DOF SCARA-type robot at 1 kHz against an aluminum plate of about 150000 N/m, with desired impedance Md=diag(20,20) kg, Bd=diag(900,900) N s/m, and Kd=diag(400,400) N/m.
Without payload, the proposed controller reportedly produces a 57.6 N impact versus 70.2 N for PB-IC, the lowest fluctuation and impedance error, while PB-IC loses contact six times.
evidence.support_scope: Section IV-D, Figs. 6-9 and Table I.

evidence.statement: With a 3.11 kg endpoint payload, the proposed controller again reportedly has the smallest position deviation, force fluctuation, and impedance error.
evidence.support_scope: Section IV-D, Figs. 10-12 and Table II.

evidence.statement: Compared with impedance control using a DOB, the proposed controller adds IMC correction for uncompensated estimation error; below 3.7 Hz its contact-force PSD is reported at about 30% of DOB's.

evidence_kind: Nonlinear multi-DOF error-channel analysis, IMC and TDE controller derivation, finite-delay frequency-response comparison, conditional L-infinity boundedness theorem, and author-reported controlled comparisons on one 2-DOF SCARA with and without payload and against DB-IC, PB-IC, IM-IC, and DOB-based impedance control.
boundary_conditions: The desired impedance is a specified Cartesian linear mass-damper-stiffness model; the method improves realization but does not learn or optimize its parameters.
The ideal perfect-control statement assumes the IMC controller is the exact inverse of its internal model and the resulting closed loop is stable.
Exact cancellation of dynamics-estimation error occurs only in the zero-feedback-delay idealization; digital implementation has unavoidable delay and residual error.
TDE assumes the lumped unknown dynamics are continuous or piecewise continuous and change little over a sufficiently small delay, normally one sampling interval.

The controller still requires a kinematic Jacobian, a selected known inertia matrix Mbar_x, measured interaction force, and delayed acceleration and input force; it is model-light, not information-free.
The stability theorem establishes L-infinity boundedness, not asymptotic convergence of impedance error, passivity, or global contact stability.
The theorem assumes desired position, velocity, acceleration, and external force are bounded in L-infinity space.

Certified stability requires the induced-norm mismatch between actual Cartesian inertia and Mbar_x to satisfy Eq. 80 for all relevant time; arbitrary payload or configuration variation is not covered.
Forgetting factors must lie between zero and one; reducing them attenuates quantization history but weakens IMC robustness correction, while increasing them shrinks the certified inertia region.
Numerical differentiation makes velocity and especially acceleration sensitive to position resolution as sampling delay decreases.
A low-pass filter changes effective TDE behavior and is described as similar to lowering Mbar_x; filter phase and contact-energy consequences are not independently analyzed here.
The experimental target is deliberately overdamped with damping ratio 5; results do not establish equivalent behavior for lightly damped or time-varying impedance.
Experiments involve one planar 2-DOF robot, one stiff aluminum wall, one approach-slide-hold trajectory, one 1 kHz implementation, and one added payload.
DB-IC and IM-IC were excluded from later comparison because their free-space errors prevented task execution, so not every reported metric is a full all-controller comparison.
PB-IC and IM-IC inner-loop gains were tuned experimentally; conclusions depend partly on the chosen tuning and hardware.
The payload test demonstrates robustness to a 3.11 kg added load, not arbitrary mass, inertia distribution, or unmodeled flexible dynamics.
Force fluctuation near 3.7 Hz is dominated by motor-driver torque ripple, limiting inference about controller performance at that frequency.
The paper does not address unilateral transition criteria, multiple contacts, frictional stick-slip, deformable or active environments, actuator saturation, or safety bounds on peak force.
assumptions: The supplied full text faithfully represents the paper and equations.
The term accuracy means small error relative to the specified impedance relation, while robustness means attenuation of robot dynamics-model error and payload variation.
Author claims of a perfect solution are interpreted only within the ideal IMC algebra; the Evidence Card preserves the finite-delay and stability-condition qualifications.
Experimental values and comparisons are treated as author-reported and not independently reproduced.
The chosen Mbar_x and forgetting factors are assumed to remain within the theorem's certified region over the tested trajectory.
No inference is made that environmental stiffness uncertainty is comprehensively solved merely because the impedance relation uses measured force.

reported: DB-IC is sensitive to dynamics modeling error, especially for small desired stiffness and large desired mass.
PB-IC improves robustness but its inner-loop dynamics distort the desired impedance and can produce oscillation or loss of contact.
IM-IC still suffers desired-impedance distortion from inner-loop dynamics.
Finite feedback delay prevents exact rejection of TDE error.
Recursive IMC feedback accumulates sensor quantization error unless forgetting or filtering is introduced.
DB-IC and IM-IC had excessive free-space position error in the experiment and could not execute the full task.
PB-IC lost contact with the wall six times and showed larger force fluctuation.
Increasing the DOB filter cutoff above 100 rad/s produced joint noise without further performance improvement.
Motor-driver torque ripple dominated remaining force fluctuation near 3.7 Hz.
Increasing the forgetting factor to enhance robustness reduces the certified stable range of Mbar_x.
inferred: Rapidly varying discontinuous contact dynamics can violate the small-delay TDE approximation and increase residual impedance error.
Acceleration estimation and one-step delay can create noise-delay tradeoffs that become more severe with lower-resolution sensing or slower sampling.
The L-infinity theorem certifies boundedness rather than safe peak interaction force, so collision safety remains unresolved.
The stable inertia region may be difficult to guarantee across large workspaces, unknown payloads, flexible transmissions, or near-singular kinematics.
The architecture improves realization of a fixed impedance but does not solve context-dependent impedance selection or generalization across tasks.
Results from a planar single-wall experiment do not establish robustness for nonlinear, multi-axis frictional, deformable, active, or multi-contact environments.
